cards.front: Why can TypeScript know that a variable contains a number without an annotation?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Type inference means the compiler works out a type from the code it can see. An initial number gives it evidence that a variable should hold numbers. You can add annotations where they explain an important boundary, such as a function input, without labeling every obvious value.

## A worked example

```ts
let attempts = 2;
attempts = 3; // allowed
// attempts = "three"; // type error
```

The first assignment establishes a numeric variable. A later string assignment conflicts with that type; the compiler does not silently change it to text.

## Picture it another way

A box delivered with pencils suggests a pencil box. A label can confirm the contents, but repeating that label on every pencil adds little information.

## A common mistake

Inference is a development aid, not a runtime guard. Data arriving from a server still needs checks even if your own variables have useful inferred types.

## Try a small exercise

With `let enabled = false`, will TypeScript accept `enabled = "yes"`?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** enabled is inferred as boolean. Assign true or false, or deliberately design a different type if text states are part of the real requirement.

cards.front: What does the vertical bar mean in the TypeScript type `string | number`?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A union describes the allowed alternatives: this value may be a string or a number. Before using an operation that works for only one alternative, check which kind you have. Operations must be safe for the possibilities remaining at that point in the code.

## A worked example

```ts
function label(id: string | number) {
  return String(id);
}
label(42); // "42"
```

String handles either allowed input. Calling a string-only method directly on id would require first checking that id is a string.

## Picture it another way

A delivery can arrive by bike or van. Instructions that require a steering wheel need to establish that this particular delivery uses the van.

## A common mistake

A union does not combine every property of every member into one object. A value that could be either shape only guarantees what those possibilities share.

## Try a small exercise

For `value: string | number`, why is `value.toUpperCase()` a type error?

<!-- recall:solution -->

The value could be a number, which has no toUpperCase method. Check `typeof value === "string"` before that call, or intentionally convert to text.

cards.front: How does a typeof check help TypeScript inside an if block?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A runtime check gives both the program and the compiler evidence about a value. Inside a branch that established a string, TypeScript allows string operations. This reduction from several possibilities to fewer possibilities is called narrowing.

## A worked example

```ts
function size(value: string | number) {
  if (typeof value === "string") {
    return value.length;
  }
  return value;
}
```

Text returns its character count here. A numeric input is returned directly because the string branch already exited.

## Picture it another way

You inspect a parcel before choosing how to carry it. Once you know it is fragile glass, the instructions can use that additional knowledge.

## A common mistake

A truthiness check also excludes values such as zero and empty text. Use a check that proves the property you actually need, instead of accidentally dropping valid inputs.

## Try a small exercise

Why is `typeof value === "number"` a better check than `if (value)` when zero is valid?

<!-- recall:solution -->

The typeof check includes zero and establishes a numeric type. A truthiness check treats zero as false, so the zero case would take the wrong path.

cards.front: What does the question mark in `nickname?: string` tell a caller?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

The object may omit nickname. Reading that property can therefore produce undefined as well as text. Decide what absence means before using it: provide a default, skip an action, or show an explicit missing state.

## A worked example

```ts
type User = { nickname?: string };
function greet(user: User) {
  return "Hi " + (user.nickname ?? "friend");
}
```

An absent nickname produces Hi friend. The fallback is used for nullish values, not for every falsy value.

## Picture it another way

An optional address line on a form may be blank because no apartment number exists. Your mailing process must handle that absence deliberately.

## A common mistake

Adding an exclamation mark to silence a possible-undefined error does not fill in missing data. A non-null assertion can hide a real crash.

## Try a small exercise

For `{ nickname: "" }`, does `user.nickname ?? "friend"` use the fallback?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** An empty string is present and is not null or undefined. If blank names should use the fallback, add that business rule explicitly, for example after trimming.

cards.front: Why is unknown useful for data you have not validated yet?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

unknown says a value exists but its usable shape has not been established. TypeScript requires evidence before allowing operations on it. any removes many of those checks. For input from outside your program, unknown keeps the need for validation visible.

## A worked example

```ts
function shout(input: unknown) {
  if (typeof input !== "string") {
    return "Expected text";
  }
  return input.toUpperCase();
}
```

Only a proven string reaches the method call. A numeric input follows the error path.

## Picture it another way

An unopened parcel has unknown contents. Checking it before plugging it in is different from declaring that everything inside is safe to use.

## A common mistake

Checking only `typeof input === "object"` is insufficient for a specific record: null is also an object under typeof, and required fields may still be missing.

## Try a small exercise

Does changing a server response from unknown to any verify its fields?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** It changes what the compiler permits, not what arrived. Check the runtime structure or use a schema validator before treating the response as trusted application data.

cards.front: Does `value as number` convert a JavaScript string into a number?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A TypeScript assertion tells the compiler to treat a value as a particular type. It does not transform or validate the value at runtime. Use a real conversion to change data, and check its result when the input might be invalid.

## A worked example

```ts
const raw: unknown = "12";
const claimed = raw as number;
console.log(typeof claimed); // "string"
const converted = Number(raw); // 12
```

claimed still contains the original text. Number runs JavaScript code that actually attempts a conversion.

## Picture it another way

Putting a label saying flour on a jar of salt does not change the contents. An assertion changes the label used during checking.

## A common mistake

Number can also produce NaN, and some inputs such as empty text convert to zero. Validate the accepted input format and result for your application.

## Try a small exercise

Can `response as User` guarantee that a downloaded object has a name field?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** The assertion performs no field checks. Validate the response at runtime before relying on User properties; an assertion alone can postpone failure until the property is used.

cards.front: What problem does a generic type parameter solve in a reusable function?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A generic lets a function describe a relationship between types without choosing one specific type in advance. For example, the first item of a list should have that list's item type. A generic preserves that connection for each call.

## A worked example

```ts
function first<T>(items: T[]): T | undefined {
  return items[0];
}
const name = first(["Ada", "Lin"]);
```

T becomes string for this call. The result is string or undefined because the list might be empty.

## Picture it another way

A coat-check ticket links your particular coat to the one returned later. The service works for many coats while preserving each handover relationship.

## A common mistake

Using any for the result loses the useful connection and allows callers to assume unsupported operations. A generic also does not make empty input impossible.

## Try a small exercise

Why should a generic first-item function include undefined in its return type?

<!-- recall:solution -->

An empty list has no first item. The type should make callers handle that possibility, unless the function instead requires a non-empty input or deliberately throws for empty lists.

cards.front: Why give each member of a TypeScript union a different kind field?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A shared field with different literal values identifies which shape is present. Checking that tag lets the compiler narrow to the matching fields. This is useful when a result can succeed with data or fail with an error, but should not have contradictory combinations.

## A worked example

```ts
type Result =
  | { kind: "ok"; value: number }
  | { kind: "error"; message: string };
function describe(r: Result) {
  return r.kind === "ok" ? String(r.value) : r.message;
}
```

The tag decides which field is safe to read.

## Picture it another way

A form marked pickup asks for a collection time; one marked delivery asks for an address. The form type determines the required details.

## A common mistake

Several optional fields can accidentally allow impossible states, such as no result and no error. A tagged union expresses the intended alternatives more clearly.

## Try a small exercise

For this union, should code read message before checking kind?

```ts
type Result =
  | { kind: "ok"; value: number }
  | { kind: "error"; message: string };
```

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** An ok result has value instead of message. Check the tag first; inside the error branch, message is guaranteed by the declared shape.

cards.front: What does readonly on a TypeScript property prevent?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

It prevents assignments to that property through a reference with that type during type checking. It communicates that this code should read rather than replace the property. It is not automatically a runtime freeze, and shallow readonly does not make every nested object immutable.

## A worked example

```ts
type Settings = { readonly theme: string };
const settings: Settings = { theme: "dark" };
// settings.theme = "light"; // type error
```

The compiler flags the assignment. JavaScript running without the type checker does not gain a new runtime guard from the annotation.

## Picture it another way

A library viewing desk asks you to read a document without editing it. The rule controls your permitted actions; it is not a physical seal on every copy.

## A common mistake

Do not assume `readonly options: { enabled: boolean }` prevents changing options.enabled. That nested field needs its own appropriate type or runtime design.

## Try a small exercise

Does a readonly array type automatically call Object.freeze on the array?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** The type restricts operations during checking. Runtime freezing is a separate JavaScript operation, with its own shallow behavior and limitations.

cards.front: How can Record help describe a TypeScript object whose keys come from a known set?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Record<Key, Value> describes properties for each allowed key with a chosen value type. When Key is a finite union, the compiler can check that each required entry exists. It is useful for small complete lookup tables such as labels for every status.

## A worked example

```ts
type Status = "open" | "closed";
const labels: Record<Status, string> = {
  open: "Still working",
  closed: "Finished",
};
```

Both statuses need text labels. Adding another status prompts you to consider its label too.

## Picture it another way

A checklist of two required rooms needs a label for each room. A complete lookup table is that checklist expressed as data.

## A common mistake

Record<string, T> does not create values for arbitrary keys at runtime. A lookup for a key that was never stored can still be missing; model and check that possibility.

## Try a small exercise

A label table uses `Record<Status, string>`, where `Status` is `"open" | "closed"`. If Status gains `"paused"`, what must the table add?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Add a paused label. With Record<Status, string>, TypeScript reports the missing required key, helping keep the table aligned with the states your program supports.

cards.front: In Python, why does range(2, 5) stop before 5?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Python ranges include the starting number and exclude the stopping number. The stop marks the boundary at which iteration ends. This convention makes it convenient to describe positions in a collection, where a length of five has positions zero through four.

## A worked example

```python
for n in range(2, 5):
    print(n)
# 2, then 3, then 4
```

The loop advances by one by default. When the next candidate reaches 5, it is outside this range.

## Picture it another way

Think of a walk that starts at marker 2 and turns back before crossing marker 5. The final marker describes a boundary, not another stop on the route.

## A common mistake

Do not add one to every stop automatically. First decide whether the requirement includes the final value; collection positions usually already fit the exclusive boundary.

## Try a small exercise

What values come from `list(range(0, 6, 2))` in Python?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**[0, 2, 4]**. Start at zero, advance by two, and stop before six. The third argument is the step size, not the number of results.

cards.front: How do the start and stop positions in a Python list slice work?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A slice such as items[start:stop] returns a new list containing positions from start up to, but excluding, stop. Leaving out start means begin at the beginning. Leaving out stop means continue to the end. The elements themselves are not deep-copied.

## A worked example

```python
letters = ["a", "b", "c", "d"]
print(letters[1:3])  # ["b", "c"]
print(letters[:2])   # ["a", "b"]
```

Positions 1 and 2 belong to the first slice. Position 3 is the excluded boundary.

## Picture it another way

Imagine cutting a strip between two ruler marks. The marks define its edges; the right-hand edge does not add another item.

## A common mistake

A new outer list can still contain references to the same nested objects. Changing a nested dictionary through the slice can affect the original list's contents.

## Try a small exercise

For `[10, 20, 30, 40]`, what does the slice `[-2:]` return?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**[30, 40]**. A negative position counts backward from the end. Start two items before the end and continue through the remaining items.

cards.front: How does Python dictionary get differ from square-bracket lookup?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Square-bracket lookup requires the key to exist and raises KeyError if it does not. get returns a default for a missing key, using None when no default is given. Choose based on whether missing data is expected or represents a bug.

```python
counts = {"apple": 2}
print(counts.get("pear", 0))  # 0
```

A receptionist can either require a reservation record or politely give a default answer when no record exists. Those are different policies for absence.

What does `{"name": None}.get("name", "Guest")` return in Python?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**None.** The key exists, so its stored value wins. If None should mean Guest, handle that case explicitly after reading the value.

cards.front: In Python, when do == and is answer different questions?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Equality with == asks whether values compare as equal. Identity with is asks whether two references point to the very same object. Two separately created lists can have equal contents without being the same list. Use is for identity checks such as comparing with None.

## A worked example

```python
a = [1, 2]
b = [1, 2]
c = a
print(a == b)  # True
print(a is b)  # False
print(a is c)  # True
```

Only c was assigned the exact list that a refers to.

## Picture it another way

Two notebooks can contain the same words while being different physical notebooks. Equality compares the writing; identity asks whether it is the same notebook.

## A common mistake

Do not use is to compare ordinary numbers or strings. Interpreter reuse of some objects can make incorrect identity comparisons appear to work in small examples.

## Try a small exercise

Which check should test whether a Python result means no value: `result == None` or `result is None`?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Use **result is None**. None is the singleton absence value. Identity is the intended question here and avoids custom equality behavior on other objects.

cards.front: Why can a Python function with a default argument of [] remember earlier calls?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Default argument values are evaluated when the function definition runs, not freshly for each call. If the default is a mutable list, calls that omit the argument use that same list. Mutating it can unexpectedly carry data into later calls.

## A worked example

```python
def collect(item, bucket=None):
    if bucket is None:
        bucket = []
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket
```

Here an omitted bucket creates a new list during each call. A caller can still intentionally supply a list to update.

## Picture it another way

A shared scratchpad left at a service counter keeps earlier notes. Handing out a fresh sheet for each visitor prevents accidental carryover.

## A common mistake

Replacing the list default with another mutable object, such as {}, has the same issue. Choose a sentinel and create the object inside the function.

## Try a small exercise

Do `collect("a")` and then `collect("b")` return one growing list here?

```python
def collect(item, bucket=None):
    if bucket is None:
        bucket = []
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket
```

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** They return ["a"] and ["b"] separately. Each omitted bucket begins as None and gets a fresh list inside that call.

cards.front: What happens when Python assigns a two-item tuple to two variable names?
cards.back:

## Plain English

```python
print(x)  # 3
print(y)  # 8
```

The first item goes to x and the second to y. The names do not change the order supplied by point.

## Picture it another way

Opening a two-compartment lunchbox and placing each item on its labeled plate resembles assigning a small bundle to separate names.

Unpacking two names from three items raises an error unless you deliberately handle the extra item. It does not silently discard values.

## Try a small exercise

What do `first, *rest = [4, 5, 6]` assign in Python?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**first is 4; rest is [5, 6].** The starred name collects the remaining items into a list, so the assignment accounts for the full input.

cards.front: Why use with when reading a file in Python?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A with statement asks a context manager to handle entry and cleanup around a block. For a file, this means the file is closed when the block ends, including when an exception interrupts it. The block makes the resource lifetime visible.

## A worked example

```python
with open("notes.txt", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
    text = handle.read()
print(text)
```

The text remains available after the block, but the file handle has been closed. This example reads an existing text file.

## Picture it another way

Borrow a room key for one meeting and return it when leaving, even if the meeting ends early. Cleanup belongs to the borrowing period.

## A common mistake

with does not mean every error is swallowed. A missing file can still raise an exception, and code should handle errors at a suitable boundary.

## Try a small exercise

If processing raises an exception inside a file with block, does the file still get closed?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**Yes.** The file context manager performs cleanup as execution exits the block. The exception normally continues outward unless some code handles it.

cards.front: How does a Python generator differ from building an entire list first?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A generator can produce one value at a time as the caller iterates. It can avoid storing every result at once, which helps for large or streaming inputs. A generator is normally consumed as you advance through it; it is not a reusable stored list.

## A worked example

```python
squares = (n * n for n in range(3))
print(next(squares))  # 0
print(list(squares))  # [1, 4]
```

next consumes the first value. The later list collects only the values that remain.

## Picture it another way

A tap provides water when opened; a bucket stores water already collected. The tap metaphor describes demand, while the bucket resembles a materialized list.

## A common mistake

After a generator is exhausted, looping over that same generator again does not restart it. Create a new generator or store the results if reuse is needed.

## Try a small exercise

Why might `list(generator)` defeat the memory advantage of using a generator?

<!-- recall:solution -->

It immediately consumes the generator and stores all remaining results in a list. Lazy production saves result storage only while the consumer also processes items incrementally.

cards.front: What belongs in a useful bug reproduction before you start editing code?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Record the starting conditions, exact actions, expected result, and actual result. Include details that affect the behavior, such as input data or whether the user is signed in. A repeatable example lets you tell whether a change actually fixes the same problem.

## A worked example

Instead of "search is broken," write: open the catalog, enter two spaces, submit, and observe a spinner that never ends. Expected: a prompt asking for a search term. Now there is a specific case to investigate and retest.

## Picture it another way

A recipe lets someone recreate a dish. A bug report needs the equivalent ingredients and steps so another person can recreate the failure.

## A common mistake

Do not include passwords or real customer records in a reproduction. Use minimal synthetic data that preserves the relevant behavior.

## Try a small exercise

A bug occurs only after refreshing a filtered page. Why include the refresh in the reproduction?

<!-- recall:solution -->

The refresh may expose missing URL state or initialization behavior. Leaving it out tests a different path and can make an apparent fix miss the real trigger.

cards.front: How does reducing a failing example help locate a bug?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Remove unrelated inputs and steps while checking that the failure still occurs. A smaller case leaves fewer possible causes and makes the important relationship easier to see. Keep the original reproduction too, because a fix should eventually work there as well.

## A worked example

A table fails with 500 records. Try a small copied set, then reduce it until one record with a missing city still fails. The investigation can now focus on handling that missing field instead of table size.

## Picture it another way

If one ingredient spoils a recipe, reducing the recipe helps isolate which ingredient matters. The reduced version must still produce the same bad result.

## A common mistake

If simplifying makes the bug disappear, you may have removed an essential condition. Restore that part and reduce somewhere else.

## Try a small exercise

Why keep retesting the failure after each simplification?

<!-- recall:solution -->

To prove the simplified example still represents the same issue. Otherwise you can end up explaining a different problem, or a case that does not fail at all.

## Plain English

A stack trace shows the chain of function calls associated with an error. Start with the error message, then inspect a relevant frame in your own code. The place that crashes is useful evidence, but the bad value may have originated earlier in the chain.

Suppose renderProfile calls formatName, which calls toUpperCase on undefined. The final method call explains the immediate failure. Then trace backward: did formatName receive missing input, or did it read the wrong property?

## Picture it another way

A delivery tracking history shows the stops a parcel passed through. The stop where damage is noticed is not necessarily where the damage began.

## A common mistake

Do not automatically edit the first library frame. Look for your call site and the values you supplied. Source maps may be needed to connect built code to source files.

## Try a small exercise

If a helper crashes on user.name, why inspect the caller as well as the helper?

<!-- recall:solution -->

The caller may supply an incomplete user or call the helper before loading finishes. Fixing the contract or timing can be more appropriate than hiding the error inside the helper.

cards.front: What does a breakpoint give you that a final error message does not?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A breakpoint pauses execution at a chosen place so you can inspect local variables, the call stack, and the next operation. Put it near where you expect a value to become wrong. Stepping then shows how that value changes instead of only revealing the final symptom.

## A worked example

For a total that doubles unexpectedly, pause before adding each item. Watch total and item.price on each pass. You may discover the loop visits every item twice or receives text instead of numbers.

## Picture it another way

A slow-motion replay lets you watch the moment a ball leaves the player's hand. A final score only tells you the result.

## A common mistake

Pausing can change timing-sensitive behavior. If a race disappears under a debugger, collect targeted timestamps or traces as another source of evidence.

## Try a small exercise

When looping over 1,000 records, how could a conditional breakpoint make debugging easier?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Pause only when a condition matches, such as the failing record ID or a negative total. You can inspect the relevant state without manually stepping through every earlier record.

cards.front: When a page shows no data, what should you inspect in the browser Network panel?

cards.front: Why can a search box briefly show results for an older query?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Requests can finish in a different order from the order they started. If every response updates the same UI without checking relevance, an old slow response can overwrite a newer one. Track which request is current or ignore results from superseded requests.

## A worked example

You type cat, then cats. The cats response arrives first and is displayed. The slower cat response arrives later and replaces it. Compare a request ID with the latest ID before applying a response; cancellation can also reduce unnecessary work.

## Picture it another way

Two food orders sent in order need not come out of the kitchen in order. The receipt identifies which waiting customer should receive each result.

## A common mistake

Adding a fixed delay does not guarantee completion order. Cancellation also needs error handling and does not always undo work already started on the server.

## Try a small exercise

Should an old response update the page just because it succeeded?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Success says the request completed, not that its result still matches the user's current intent. Apply it only if it belongs to the active query or state.

cards.front: A price parser used to reject surrounding spaces. How would you turn that bug into a regression test?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Capture the specific input that failed and check the intended result: if surrounding spaces are allowed, parsing " 12 " should produce 12. The test should fail against the old broken behavior and pass with the fix. It reminds future changes to preserve this case.

## A worked example

A price parser rejected " 12 ". If surrounding spaces are allowed, add a test expecting 12 from that input. Also retain a rejection case for truly invalid text so the fix does not simply accept everything.

## Picture it another way

After repairing a leaky seam, mark that location on the inspection checklist. Future inspections then explicitly cover the previously weak spot.

## A common mistake

A test that only checks the new helper was called can pass even when the user-visible bug remains. Assert the result that matters.

## Try a small exercise

Why is it useful to confirm the regression test fails before applying the fix?

<!-- recall:solution -->

It shows the test can detect the original defect. Without that check, a passing test may merely exercise unrelated code and provide false confidence.

cards.front: What should a short engineering update about a bug fix communicate?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Describe the trigger, the cause you established, the changed behavior, and how you checked it. Keep observed facts separate from remaining uncertainty. Another engineer should understand both why the change helps and what your verification covered.

"Refreshing a filtered list lost the selected category because initialization ignored the URL. The page now reads that parameter on load. Checked direct links, refresh, and an unknown category." Each sentence gives a reviewer useful evidence.

Avoid claiming that all possible failures are fixed when you tested one path. State the relevant coverage and any known unresolved condition precisely.

<!-- recall:solution -->

It gives no way to assess whether the original failure was addressed. Concrete trigger and test details let someone reproduce the result and judge the scope of the fix.

cards.front: How do arrange, act, and assert make a test easier to understand?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Arrange creates the starting data and conditions. Act performs the behavior you want to check. Assert compares the result with the expected outcome. Keeping these jobs recognizable makes it easier to see what a failing test is actually telling you.

## A worked example

```js
const cart = [{ price: 3 }, { price: 4 }]; // arrange
const total = sumPrices(cart);           // act
expect(total).toBe(7);                   // assert
```

sumPrices is the function under test. The assertion states the concrete outcome rather than repeating its implementation.

## Picture it another way

Set up a bowling lane, roll the ball, then count the pins. Mixing setup changes into the counting step makes the result harder to interpret.

## A common mistake

If the assertion calculates its expected result with the same algorithm as the implementation, both can share the same mistake. Use independently reasoned expectations.

## Try a small exercise

In a login test, is creating an existing user usually arrange or assert?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**Arrange.** It establishes the conditions for the login attempt. Assert should check the resulting session, response, or visible logged-in state after the action.

cards.front: For a rule that starts at 18, why test 17, 18, and 19?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Boundary tests focus on the values where behavior changes. One value below, exactly at, and one above a cutoff distinguish common comparison mistakes. They are often more informative than testing several values far from the decision point.

## A worked example

If eligibility means age >= 18, then 17 is false, 18 is true, and 19 is true. An accidental > instead of >= changes only the exact boundary among these cases, so the test at 18 catches it.

## Picture it another way

When checking a doorway's height, measuring near the top edge is more useful than confirming many tiny objects fit underneath.

## A common mistake

Boundary tests do not replace other classes of input. Consider absence, wrong types, and impossible values separately where the function is responsible for validating them.

## Try a small exercise

A field allows at most 20 characters. Which lengths make a useful boundary set?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**19, 20, and 21.** The first two should be accepted and 21 rejected. Also consider an empty input if a separate required-field rule applies.

cards.front: What does partitioning inputs mean when choosing test cases?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Group inputs that should follow the same rule, then choose representative cases from different groups. This gives more useful coverage than many nearly identical examples. Add boundary cases where groups meet, because that is where classification errors often occur.

## A worked example

For an email field, possible groups include missing input, clearly invalid format, and accepted format. Ten ordinary accepted addresses may all exercise the same path while never checking how an invalid value is handled.

## Picture it another way

Testing one road in every neighborhood tells you more about a city than testing ten neighboring driveways on the same street.

## A common mistake

Your groups are a model of the requirements, not a guarantee. New bug reports can reveal a meaningful group you had missed.

## Try a small exercise

Why might an empty list and a one-item list both deserve tests for an average function?

<!-- recall:solution -->

They expose different behavior: an empty list needs a defined policy, while one item should return that item's value. Ordinary multi-item examples do not establish either case.

cards.front: What can an integration test catch that an isolated function test might miss?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

An integration test checks cooperating pieces across a real boundary, such as an API handler and a database. It can reveal mismatched field names, transaction behavior, or wiring mistakes even when each isolated helper appears correct.

## A worked example

A helper correctly creates `{ displayName: "Ada" }`, but the storage layer expects display_name. A test that writes through the handler and reads the saved record exercises the connection where that mismatch matters.

## Picture it another way

Testing a plug and a socket separately does not prove they fit together. An integration test checks that connection.

## A common mistake

Connecting every production dependency makes tests slower and harder to control. Choose the specific boundary whose real behavior provides useful confidence, with isolated test data.

## Try a small exercise

If a query helper is mocked to return a valid user, does that test prove the real SQL query works?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** The mock bypasses the query. You need a test that actually exercises the query against an appropriate test database to check that integration.

cards.front: What is a test double, and why replace a dependency in a test?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A test double stands in for a real dependency so the test can control its behavior. For example, a fake email sender can record attempted messages without sending them. This makes failures repeatable and keeps unrelated network behavior out of a focused test.

## A worked example

A password-reset test supplies an email sender that records its inputs. The test checks that the reset flow requests one message for the expected user, while separate integration checks cover the actual provider connection.

## Picture it another way

A practice steering wheel lets you rehearse a specific maneuver without depending on weather and traffic. It is useful only within the skills it represents.

## A common mistake

A double can drift from the real contract. Keep its behavior realistic, and do not mock away the very boundary the test is intended to verify.

## Try a small exercise

Why should a payment-flow unit test not send a real payment merely to check local validation?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Validation can be tested before the external boundary using a controlled double. Real side effects add cost and risk without helping verify that local rule; provider integration needs a suitable separate test environment.

cards.front: Why should a UI test often locate a button by its accessible name?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A visible, accessible name connects the test to how a person identifies the control. It also avoids tying the test to incidental styling classes or component structure. Interact through the interface and assert the behavior the user depends on.

A test clicks the button named Save and waits for "Saved" to appear. Renaming a private CSS class should not break this test. Removing the button's meaningful label should draw attention because it changes how the control is found.

## Picture it another way

A driving test asks whether you can stop at a sign, not what color the mechanic painted a hidden bracket.

## A common mistake

A user-facing locator is not a complete accessibility audit. Keyboard behavior, focus movement, and other requirements still need appropriate checks.

## Try a small exercise

If a refactor changes internal state variable names but preserves the interface, should a behavior test normally fail?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** A test centered on observable behavior should survive that refactor. Failures tied only to private names often indicate unnecessary coupling to implementation details.

cards.front: Why is a fixed sleep a fragile way to test asynchronous UI behavior?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A sleep guesses how long the operation needs. It may be too short on a busy machine and unnecessarily long on a fast one. Prefer waiting for the specific result with a bounded timeout, such as the appearance of a saved message.

## A worked example

After clicking Save, wait until the UI displays Saved, then assert the updated value. If the condition never arrives before the deadline, the test fails with a meaningful missing outcome instead of randomly checking too soon.

## Picture it another way

Wait for the oven's ready signal instead of guessing that every oven warms up in exactly ten seconds.

## A common mistake

An unbounded wait can hang forever. Use a reasonable deadline and make the condition precise enough that an old unrelated message cannot satisfy it.

## Try a small exercise

Why should an async assertion wait for the new record's name rather than just any row?

<!-- recall:solution -->

An old row may already exist, allowing the test to pass before saving finishes. The expected new name ties the wait to the operation being tested.

cards.front: How can passing a clock into code make time-based behavior easier to test?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A controllable clock lets the test choose the current time instead of depending on the real date or waiting for time to pass. You can check exact expiration boundaries and scheduling behavior quickly and repeatably.

## A worked example

```js
function isExpired(expiresAt, now) {
  return now >= expiresAt;
}
expect(isExpired(1000, 999)).toBe(false);
expect(isExpired(1000, 1000)).toBe(true);
```

All values use the same time unit. The test controls both sides of the comparison.

## Picture it another way

A rehearsal clock can jump directly to midnight so you can practice what happens then without staying awake until the real midnight.

## A common mistake

Replacing the current date may not also advance timers. Understand whether your test controls wall-clock readings, scheduled callbacks, or both.

## Try a small exercise

Why can a test using the real current date fail only around midnight?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Its setup and assertion may cross a date boundary or depend on a local timezone. Fix the reference time and test the intended boundary explicitly.

cards.front: What is a property worth testing for a sorting function?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A property is a rule that should hold across many inputs, not only one expected example. A sorted result should be ordered and should contain the same items with the same counts. Properties can expose cases you did not think to write by hand.

## A worked example

For input [3, 1, 3], checking only that the output is ordered would allow [1, 3], which lost an item. Check ordering, length, and item frequencies so duplicates and contents are preserved.

## Picture it another way

Inspecting a packed suitcase requires checking both neat arrangement and that every item arrived. Tidiness alone cannot detect a missing shirt.

## A common mistake

A weak property can pass for a useless implementation. For example, always returning an empty list satisfies the rule "no adjacent items are out of order."

## Try a small exercise

Why is "output length equals input length" insufficient to validate a sort?

<!-- recall:solution -->

An implementation could return the wrong values in the right quantity. Combine length with ordering and preservation of each item's frequency, plus representative examples.

cards.front: Why can tests pass individually but fail when run together?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

They may share mutable state such as database rows, storage, mocks, or timers. One test leaves a condition that changes another test's starting point. Each test should establish and clean up the state it depends on so execution order is not part of its hidden contract.

## A worked example

A test stores a signed-in user in local storage. The next test expects the signed-out page but never clears storage. Resetting the owned test state before each case makes both starting conditions explicit.

## Picture it another way

Each cooking student needs a prepared workstation. Leftover ingredients from the previous student can change the next recipe without appearing in its instructions.

## A common mistake

Avoid clearing real user data or shared environments as test cleanup. Use isolated test storage and databases that the suite owns.

## Try a small exercise

A failure disappears when tests run in a different order. What should you inspect first?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Look for shared state and incomplete cleanup: module variables, persisted rows, mock behavior, event listeners, and fake timers. Order sensitivity is strong evidence of an unintended dependency between tests.

cards.front: Why does a text field need a label even if it has placeholder text?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A label tells people what information belongs in the field and can provide its accessible name. Placeholder text can disappear while typing and often works better as an example. A persistent label lets people review a completed form without guessing what each value means.

## A worked example

```html
<label for="city">City</label>
<input id="city" name="city" placeholder="For example, Leeds">
```

The for value matches the input ID, connecting the label to the control. The placeholder offers an example without carrying the field's entire meaning.

## Picture it another way

A folder keeps its label after you put papers inside. A form field should also keep its identity after you enter data.

## A common mistake

Nearby text is not necessarily a programmatically associated label. Verify the actual connection rather than relying only on visual proximity.

## Try a small exercise

What should match between `<label for="email">` and its input?

<!-- recall:solution -->

The input's **id should be email**. That connection associates the label with the input. The name attribute serves form submission and does not replace this ID relationship.

cards.front: Why should an interactive element keep a visible keyboard focus indicator?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Focus shows which control will receive keyboard input. A visible indicator helps people navigate without a mouse and know what Enter or Space will activate. Removing the default outline requires providing another clear indicator, not leaving focus invisible.

## A worked example

```css
button:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid #14532d;
  outline-offset: 3px;
}
```

The outline surrounds the focused button without changing the layout. Check that its color and position remain visible against the surrounding design.

## Picture it another way

A reading cursor shows where the next typed character goes. Keyboard focus provides the equivalent location signal for interactive controls.

## A common mistake

Hover styling alone is insufficient: keyboard users may never move a pointer over the focused control. Test by actually tabbing through the page.

## Try a small exercise

A button looks selected on mouse hover but has no change when tabbed to. What is missing?

<!-- recall:solution -->

A visible keyboard focus state. Add or restore a clear focus indicator, then confirm that it is visible and that the control can be activated from the keyboard.

cards.front: Where should keyboard focus go when a modal dialog opens and closes?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Opening a modal should move focus into an appropriate place in the dialog, and keyboard interaction should remain within the active modal. Closing normally returns focus to the control that opened it, if that control still exists. This keeps the user's location understandable.

## A worked example

A Rename button opens a dialog. Focus enters the name field; Tab moves among the dialog controls. Cancel closes the dialog and focus returns to Rename. A user can complete the flow without hunting through the background page.

## Picture it another way

Entering a service booth moves your conversation inside it. When you leave, you return to the place in the queue where you started.

## A common mistake

Adding aria-modal alone does not implement focus movement or prevent background interaction. Use a suitable dialog implementation and test its actual behavior.

## Try a small exercise

After closing a dialog, why is sending focus to the top of the page usually unhelpful?

<!-- recall:solution -->

It loses the user's working position and forces extra navigation. Return focus to the opener or another logical next control if the opener was removed by the completed action.

cards.front: What makes a form validation message useful to a beginner user?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Name the field, explain the problem in ordinary language, and tell the person how to fix it. Keep their entered data available. Associate the message with the field so assistive technology can connect the explanation to the affected control.

## A worked example

Instead of "Invalid," show "Choose a delivery date on or after today" beside the date field. Mark the field invalid and reference the message with aria-describedby. The wording explains a rule the person can act on.

## Picture it another way

A helpful teacher points to the step to correct and explains the rule. A red mark without an explanation leaves the student guessing.

## A common mistake

Color alone should not carry the error meaning. Add text, and do not clear the entire form after one invalid field.

## Try a small exercise

Why is "Something went wrong" a weak response to a password that is too short?

<!-- recall:solution -->

It hides a specific fix the user can make. State the applicable password requirement clearly, while reserving generic messages for cases where details would reveal sensitive account information.

cards.front: Why should a data view distinguish loading, an empty result, and an error?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

These states imply different actions. Loading means the outcome is still pending. Empty means the request succeeded but found no matching items. Error means the outcome could not be obtained. Clear states prevent people from interpreting a failure as a true absence of data.

## A worked example

A search view can show "Searching…", then either result cards, "No matches for this search", or "Could not load results. Try again." Each message describes what is known rather than displaying the same blank panel for every case.

## Picture it another way

A closed shop, an open shop with no stock, and a shop whose status you cannot check are different situations. An empty window cannot explain all three.

## A common mistake

Do not convert every caught exception into an empty array and present it as success. That hides failures and can mislead users about their stored information.

## Try a small exercise

If a network request fails, should the app tell the user "You have no saved notes"?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** The app has not established that. Show that notes could not be loaded, retain any appropriate known data, and offer a relevant retry path.

cards.front: How should an image's purpose influence its alternative text?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Alternative text should convey the information or function the image provides in that context. A decorative image can use empty alt text so it does not add noise. A functional image, such as an image inside a link, needs an understandable action or destination.

## A worked example

A chart showing sales increasing needs a text explanation of the important trend and accessible data as appropriate. A decorative flourish beside an already labeled heading can use `alt=""`. Describing both as "image" helps with neither purpose.

## Picture it another way

When explaining a slide over the phone, describe what the listener needs to understand, not every decorative shape on the slide.

## A common mistake

Do not put important chart information only in a very long alt attribute. Complex content may need nearby explanation or a table that everyone can use.

## Try a small exercise

A magnifying-glass image is the only content of a search button. What name does the control need?

<!-- recall:solution -->

An accessible name such as **Search** that explains the action. Naming it "magnifying glass" describes the drawing but leaves the button's function less clear.

cards.front: Why are flexible widths helpful when a page must work on a phone?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A flexible layout uses available space and lets content wrap instead of assuming one screen width. Combine that flexibility with sensible maximum widths and breakpoints where the content needs them. Long words, zoom, and translated labels also affect the space required.

```css
.panel {
  width: 100%;
  max-width: 40rem;
  box-sizing: border-box;
}
```

## Picture it another way

An adjustable bookshelf fits several rooms while keeping shelves at a usable size. A fixed oversized cabinet may block the doorway in a smaller room.

## A common mistake

Hiding all horizontal overflow can conceal clipped controls. Find the element forcing the width and adapt it; code samples may need their own horizontal scrolling area.

## Try a small exercise

A long code line pushes the entire phone page sideways. What is a useful local fix?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Constrain the code block within the layout and let that block scroll horizontally or wrap where appropriate. Keep the surrounding text and controls within the viewport.

cards.front: Why should touch controls have generous hit areas and spacing?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A fingertip covers more area than a pointer, especially while walking or using one hand. Larger hit areas and separation reduce accidental activation. The visible icon can be small while the button around it provides a comfortable area to tap.

## A worked example

A 16-pixel edit icon can sit inside a button with padding that makes the interactive area roughly 44 pixels high or larger. Keep adjacent delete and edit actions distinct, then test on a narrow screen with realistic text sizes.

## Picture it another way

Large, separated elevator buttons are easier to select than tiny tightly packed switches. The surrounding touch area matters as much as the symbol.

## A common mistake

Do not expose essential actions only on hover. Touch devices may not offer that interaction, and keyboard users need a discoverable path too.

## Try a small exercise

If a tiny icon has a large visual margin but no button padding, is the margin necessarily clickable?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** The actual interactive element determines the hit area. Use appropriate padding or dimensions on the button itself and verify its boundaries in the browser.

cards.front: What different jobs do an HTTP request's method, URL, headers, and body perform?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

The method expresses the kind of operation, and the URL identifies the target. Headers carry metadata such as accepted formats or credentials. A body can carry submitted data. Reading these parts separately helps you diagnose a request and describe its contract clearly.

## A worked example

A POST to /notes with Content-Type: application/json and body `{ "text": "Review closures" }` asks the server to process submitted note data. The path names the resource area; the body carries the new text.

## Picture it another way

A parcel has a destination, handling instructions, and contents. Confusing the label with the contents makes delivery harder to reason about.

A body is not automatically JSON merely because the client sent text that resembles an object. The content type and server parsing rules need to agree.

<!-- recall:solution -->

Inspect the Content-Type header and the actual transmitted body. Confirm valid JSON encoding and the field shape the endpoint expects, instead of assuming the client's original object was sent correctly.

cards.front: How do path parameters and query parameters commonly differ in an API?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A path often identifies a resource, while query parameters refine a request with filters, sorting, or pagination. This is a design convention that makes URLs easier to read. The server must still validate both kinds of input.

`/users/42` identifies a particular user. `/users?active=true&limit=10` asks for a filtered collection. The value "true" arrives through URL parsing as text unless your framework deliberately converts it.

Do not assume a numeric-looking path or query value is already a validated number. Parse it and apply the allowed range and format.

cards.front: Why should a GET endpoint avoid performing an action such as deleting a record?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

GET has safe semantics: the caller is asking to retrieve information, not requesting a state-changing action. Browsers, crawlers, and intermediaries may fetch or repeat such requests. Encoding deletion in a GET URL makes ordinary retrieval behavior dangerous.

## A worked example

A link to `/notes/7` can display a note. Deleting it should use an appropriately designed mutation endpoint with authorization and request protections. A crawler following a display link should not delete the note.

## Picture it another way

Opening a product catalog should not place an order. Looking and acting are different commitments even if both involve the same product.

## A common mistake

Safe does not mean nothing whatsoever changes internally: access logging may occur. The distinction is whether the client requested a meaningful mutation through the operation.

## Try a small exercise

Why is a GET link such as `/account/delete` a poor deletion design?

<!-- recall:solution -->

A browser or automated fetcher may visit it as an ordinary retrieval. Deletion needs an explicit mutation operation, authorization, and appropriate protections against unintended requests.

cards.front: What broad difference separates HTTP 2xx, 4xx, and 5xx responses?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

2xx indicates successful handling at the HTTP level. 4xx indicates a problem with the request in relation to the resource or its rules. 5xx indicates the server could not fulfill an apparently valid request because of a server-side failure. Specific codes refine those meanings.

## A worked example

A successful retrieval might return 200. An unknown resource might return 404. A temporary service failure might return 503. The response body can add application details, but clients should not have to treat every outcome as an indistinguishable 200.

## Picture it another way

A service desk can say completed, please correct the request, or our equipment is unavailable. Those categories suggest different next steps.

## A common mistake

The broad category does not determine a safe retry policy by itself. Some failures need corrected input, some may be transient, and repeated mutations may duplicate effects.

## Try a small exercise

If a client sends a required field in the wrong format, is a generic 500 usually the clearest response?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Use an appropriate documented client-error response and a useful validation message. A 500 incorrectly suggests an unexpected server failure rather than a correctable request problem.

cards.front: Why does a JavaScript fetch call need to check response.ok?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

fetch can fulfill its promise when an HTTP response arrives even if the status is an error such as 404. Promise rejection usually concerns failures such as a network problem or cancellation. Check the HTTP outcome before treating the body as a successful application result.

## A worked example

```js
const response = await fetch("/api/notes");
if (!response.ok) {
  throw new Error("Could not load notes");
}
const notes = await response.json();
```

This checks status before parsing the success payload. Real code also needs a place to handle the thrown error.

## Picture it another way

Receiving a reply from a shop does not mean your order succeeded. The reply may explain that the requested item does not exist.

## A common mistake

Even a successful status can carry malformed JSON or an unexpected shape. Handle parsing failures and validate the data needed by the application.

## Try a small exercise

Will `catch` alone necessarily detect a fetch response with status 404?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** fetch generally resolves with that response. Inspect response.ok or status and explicitly handle the HTTP error; catch handles rejected operations and errors you throw.

cards.front: Why can response.json() fail even after an HTTP request succeeds?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A delivered envelope may intentionally be empty. Receiving it successfully does not mean there is a letter inside to read.

## A common mistake

A proxy or login redirect can produce HTML where your API client expected JSON. Inspect status, final response details, and content type when parsing unexpectedly fails.

## Try a small exercise

After a documented 204 response, should the client require a JSON object before showing success?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** 204 means there is no response content. Treat the documented outcome as success without JSON parsing, while handling other status cases according to the endpoint contract.

cards.front: Why should an API usually return a bounded page instead of every record?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A page limits transfer size, memory use, and work per request. The response should give clients a defined way to request more results. This keeps a growing dataset from silently turning one ordinary screen load into an enormous operation.

## A worked example

A notes endpoint returns at most 20 items and a nextCursor when more are available. The client requests another page using that cursor. The server caps allowed page sizes even if a caller asks for millions of items.

## Picture it another way

Borrowing a tray of books at a time is manageable. Delivering the entire library whenever someone opens the catalog is not.

## A common mistake

Pagination needs a defined ordering. If tied or shifting positions are not handled, people may see duplicated or skipped records between pages.

## Try a small exercise

Why should the server enforce a maximum limit even if the UI only offers 20 and 50?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Clients can bypass the UI and send arbitrary values. The server owns resource limits and must validate the request independently of the controls shown in one frontend.

cards.front: Why can renaming a JSON response field break an otherwise working client?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Clients rely on the agreed names, types, and meanings of response fields. Renaming a field changes that contract even when the server's internal data is identical. Coordinate breaking changes or provide a compatibility period so existing callers still work.

## A worked example

A phone app reads displayName. If the server changes it to name overnight, the old app may show a blank label. A transition can supply both fields while clients migrate, then remove the old field under a defined versioning policy.

## Picture it another way

Changing a familiar street name without updating maps can leave travelers lost even though the street itself is still there.

## A common mistake

Even adding a field is not guaranteed harmless for every client: some validate exact shapes. Understand the real consumer contract rather than assuming all clients ignore unknown fields.

## Try a small exercise

If a numeric price field changes from dollars to cents but keeps its name, is that a contract change?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**Yes.** Meaning is part of the contract. A client may now display a value one hundred times too large; document units and coordinate the change explicitly.

cards.front: How can an idempotency key help when a client is unsure whether a create request succeeded?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

The client assigns one key to a logical action and reuses it for retries of that same action. The server records the key and outcome so repeated attempts can refer to the original result instead of creating additional effects. Correct implementation requires coordinated storage and a defined key lifetime.

## A worked example

Creating an export job succeeds, but the response is lost. A retry with the same key should return the original job, within the API's guarantees. A genuinely new export receives a new key. The server should reject incompatible payload reuse.

## Picture it another way

A claim ticket identifies one submitted repair. Asking about the same ticket again should not create a second repair order.

## A common mistake

A fresh random key for every retry defeats deduplication. A shared key for unrelated actions can suppress legitimate work. Scope keys to the user or tenant as appropriate.

## Try a small exercise

Should the retry of one timed-out order submission reuse its original idempotency key?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**Yes, under that API's documented contract.** It represents the same intended action. A new key would make it look like another action and could allow a duplicate order.

cards.front: What should a client consider when an API responds with 429 Too Many Requests?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

The server is applying a request limit. The client should reduce pressure, use any documented retry guidance, and show an appropriate waiting or retry state. Immediate repeated requests can keep the client limited and add unnecessary load.

## A worked example

A search client receives 429 with a Retry-After value. It can defer an eligible retry for that duration within a bounded policy and avoid repeatedly sending the same request. Retry-After may be expressed as seconds or an HTTP date.

## Picture it another way

A busy counter asks customers to wait before trying again. Knocking repeatedly does not create more capacity behind the counter.

## A common mistake

Do not blindly retry every operation after waiting. Consider whether it is safe to repeat, whether the user still needs it, and the total time budget.

## Try a small exercise

Why should a rate-limited search avoid retrying once the user has typed a different query?

<!-- recall:solution -->

The original result is no longer relevant. Cancel or discard superseded work and use the available request budget for the current intent instead of stale searches.

cards.front: Before writing an aggregate query, why define what one output row should represent?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A row might represent an order, a customer, or a customer-month. That level of detail determines grouping and which joins are appropriate. Stating it first helps avoid combining unrelated quantities or accidentally returning several rows when the caller expects one.

## A worked example

For "total spending per customer," one output row represents a customer. Group order amounts by customer_id. Adding order_id to that grouping changes the level to individual orders and no longer produces one total per customer.

## Picture it another way

A school report can have one row per student or one per class. Mixing those meanings makes averages and totals hard to interpret.

## A common mistake

Do not select extra grouping columns just to make a SQL error disappear. Each extra column may change what a row means.

## Try a small exercise

If a report needs one row per day, what happens if you also group by individual event ID?

<!-- recall:solution -->

You split each day into separate event groups, losing the intended daily total. Group at the requested level and aggregate the event values that belong to each day.

cards.back:

## Plain English

A join produces a result row for each matching pair. One order with three line items appears three times in that joined result. Summing the order's already-complete total then counts it three times. Understand the relationship before aggregating.

An order total is 30 and has two matching item rows. After the join, the total column appears as 30 and 30, so SUM gives 60. Aggregate at the order level or use the appropriate line-item amounts instead.

Photocopying an invoice once per package does not create additional money owed. Counting every copy as a new invoice overstates the bill.

SUM(DISTINCT total) is not a general repair: two different orders can legitimately have the same total and one would be lost.

cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A left join keeps left-side rows without a match by filling right-side columns with NULL. A later WHERE condition keeps only rows where its condition is true. If that condition rejects the NULL-filled rows, those unmatched left rows disappear.

## A worked example

cards.front: When should a SQL condition use HAVING instead of WHERE?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

WHERE filters input rows before grouping. HAVING filters the groups produced by aggregation. If the condition depends on a group's total or count, it normally belongs in HAVING. Conditions about individual input rows usually belong in WHERE.

## A worked example

```sql
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid'
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;
```

First keep paid orders, then group them, then keep customers with at least three of those orders.

## Picture it another way

First select eligible ballots, then count them by candidate, then keep candidates whose total passes a threshold. The two filtering stages ask different questions.

Filtering out individual small purchases before summing is different from filtering customers whose overall spending is small. Place the rule at its intended level.

<!-- recall:solution -->

**HAVING.** The average belongs to a department group. WHERE would filter individual employee rows before that average is calculated, changing the population being averaged.

cards.front: How does a SQL window function differ from grouping rows with GROUP BY?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A window function computes across a related set of rows while retaining the individual result rows. GROUP BY normally collapses rows into groups. Window functions help when you need both each item and a comparison or calculation over its peers.

## A worked example

```sql
SELECT name, team_id,
       COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY team_id) AS team_size
FROM members;
```

Each member still gets a row. team_size repeats the count for that member's team beside their name.

## Picture it another way

Each student keeps an individual report card with the class size written beside their own information. You did not replace the class with one summary card.

## A common mistake

Ordering and window frames affect functions such as running sums. Learn the specific frame rather than assuming every window automatically means the entire partition.

Five members belong to one team. How many rows does this query return for that team?

```sql
SELECT name, team_id,
       COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY team_id) AS team_size
FROM members;
```

<!-- recall:solution -->

**Five rows**, each showing team_size as 5. A grouped team-count query would instead usually return one summary row for that team.

cards.front: What rule does a database foreign key express?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A foreign key links values in one table to an allowed key in another table, preventing invalid references under the defined constraint. For example, an order's customer ID should refer to a real customer. Nullability and deletion behavior are separate decisions.

## A worked example

If orders.customer_id references customers.id, inserting a non-NULL customer ID that does not exist is rejected. Deleting a referenced customer may be blocked or trigger a configured action such as cascading, depending on the schema.

## Picture it another way

A library loan card should name a member who exists in the membership register. The reference connects records rather than copying all membership details.

## A common mistake

Do not assume a foreign key automatically selects the right business deletion policy. Cascading can remove many dependent records, so choose that behavior deliberately.

## Try a small exercise

Does a foreign key alone guarantee that every order has a customer when customer_id is nullable?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** A nullable foreign-key column can generally store NULL. Add the appropriate NOT NULL constraint if the business rule requires a customer on every order.

cards.front: Why can copying a customer's current address into many unrelated rows cause update problems?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Duplicated current facts can drift when one copy changes and another does not. A normalized design stores the fact in a suitable authoritative record and references it where needed. Some duplication is intentional, such as preserving an order's historical shipping address.

## A worked example

Keep a customer's current contact email on the customer record. When it changes, update that record. An invoice may deliberately store the billing details used when it was issued, because its purpose is historical rather than current.

## Picture it another way

A shared address book is easier to maintain than many unofficial scraps of the same current address. A dated receipt, however, should preserve what was true at the time.

## A common mistake

Do not remove every duplicate-looking field blindly. Ask whether it represents a current shared fact, a historical snapshot, or a measured performance tradeoff.

## Try a small exercise

Should changing a customer's current address automatically rewrite the shipping address on an already-delivered order?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Usually **no**: that order records where it was shipped at the time. The historical address and the customer's current address serve different purposes even if they once matched.

cards.front: What can a query execution plan tell you about a slow database read?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A plan describes how the database intends to retrieve and combine rows. It can reveal scans, joins, sorting, and estimated amounts of work. Compare the plan with the query and data distribution before deciding that adding an index will solve the problem.

## A worked example

A query requesting most rows in a small table may reasonably use a sequential scan. An index is not automatically faster: following many separate index entries can cost more than reading the table in order.

## Picture it another way

A map of the delivery route explains why the trip is long. Buying a faster bicycle will not help if the main issue is visiting every address unnecessarily.

## A common mistake

EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement to measure it. Use an appropriate test environment and understand effects before applying it, especially to writes.

## Try a small exercise

Is seeing a sequential scan enough evidence that a query plan is bad?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** It can be efficient for small tables or queries needing a large share of rows. Assess actual workload, row counts, filtering, and measured cost rather than treating one plan label as a defect.

cards.front: Why can binary floating-point be awkward for exact decimal amounts?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Many decimal fractions cannot be represented exactly in binary floating-point, so arithmetic can accumulate tiny rounding differences. Exact decimal database types or integer minor units can fit money-like amounts better, with explicit currency, scale, and rounding rules.

## A worked example

```js
0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3; // false
10 + 20 === 30;    // true
```

The integer example could represent minor units in a deliberately chosen scale. It does not automatically handle currencies with different fractional rules or values outside the safe integer range.

## Picture it another way

Measuring with a ruler whose marks do not match your required fractions forces approximation. Choose units and a measuring tool suited to the required precision.

## A common mistake

Do not round at arbitrary intermediate steps or assume every currency has two decimal places. Define the representation and rounding policy across storage, calculation, and display.

## Try a small exercise

If you store an amount as integer minor units, what additional meaning must the system preserve?

<!-- recall:solution -->

The currency and unit scale, plus relevant rounding and range rules. The integer 123 alone does not tell a caller whether it means 123 units, 1.23 units, or something else.

cards.front: Why is checking that a user is signed in insufficient before returning a private note by ID?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Signing in establishes identity, but the server must also check whether that identity may access this particular note. A caller can change an ID in a request. Restrict the lookup by the authenticated user's permissions or ownership rules before returning private data.

## A worked example

For a personal-note app, query for the requested note ID together with the owner ID from the verified session. Do not accept an owner ID supplied by the browser as proof of ownership. Shared notes need an explicit sharing policy instead.

## Picture it another way

A building pass proves who you are; it does not give you permission to open every tenant's mailbox.

## A common mistake

Hiding an Edit button is useful UI behavior but does not enforce server permissions. Direct requests can bypass the page entirely.

## Try a small exercise

If note IDs are long random strings, can the API skip checking ownership?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Hard-to-guess identifiers can reduce guessing but do not grant permission. A leaked or shared ID must still be subject to the server's authorization rules.

cards.front: What does least privilege mean for an application account?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Give an identity only the permissions needed for its job, within an appropriate scope. A reporting service that reads data should not automatically get permission to delete tables. Smaller permission sets reduce the effects of mistakes and compromised credentials.

## A worked example

A background thumbnail worker needs access to specific image inputs and output storage. It does not need full administrative access to user accounts. Separate roles make that distinction enforceable.

## Picture it another way

A cleaner needs a key to the rooms they clean, not the key to every safe in the building.

## A common mistake

Do not assume a role remains appropriate forever. New features and old unused permissions can change the actual access needed; review scope when responsibilities change.

## Try a small exercise

A dashboard only reads reports. Why avoid giving its database account schema-changing privileges?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Those privileges do not support its job and increase the damage a bug or stolen credential could cause. An appropriately scoped read role better matches the required behavior.
