cards.front: Why is a server API secret unsafe when bundled into frontend JavaScript?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Code and configuration delivered to a browser can be inspected by the person using it. A private credential included in that bundle is therefore exposed. Keep server secrets in an appropriate server environment and have the browser use an authorized server API.

## A worked example

A weather-provider secret used for billed server requests belongs behind your backend. The browser calls your endpoint, which enforces its own access and request limits. A public publishable key is different only when the provider explicitly designed it to be public.

## Picture it another way

Writing a safe combination on a customer receipt does not keep it secret just because the receipt was printed by trusted staff.

## A common mistake

An environment variable is not automatically secret: build tools can insert selected variables into browser assets. Inspect what is actually shipped and follow the provider's key model.

## Try a small exercise

Does minifying JavaScript protect a private API key embedded in it?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Minification changes presentation, not access. Anyone receiving the bundle can recover its values; move the private credential to the proper server boundary and rotate it if exposed.

cards.front: Why should a server use a dedicated password-hashing algorithm rather than plain text or a fast general hash?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A password verifier should make offline guessing expensive if the database leaks. Dedicated password-hashing schemes use a salt and configurable work costs suited to that purpose. Use a maintained implementation and current parameters rather than inventing your own scheme.

## A worked example

At registration, the password library produces a stored verifier including algorithm settings and salt information. At login, its verify operation checks the submitted password against that verifier. The server does not need to recover the original password.

## Picture it another way

The system keeps a way to check the answer, not a readable copy of the answer. The checking process is intentionally costly enough to slow mass guessing.

## A common mistake

A fast hash such as plain SHA-256 is not an appropriate standalone password-storage scheme. Hashing also does not replace rate limits, secure transport, or account recovery design.

## Try a small exercise

Should a password-reset feature email the user their existing password?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** The system should not be able to retrieve it from a proper verifier. Use a secure, time-limited reset process that allows the user to choose a new password.

cards.front: Why is inserting a user comment as HTML different from displaying it as text?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

HTML insertion asks the browser to interpret markup, which can introduce unwanted elements or executable behavior. Text insertion displays characters as data. Use the framework's safe text rendering for ordinary comments; rich HTML needs a suitable sanitization policy and library.

## A worked example

```js
commentElement.textContent = userComment;
```

Here commentElement is an existing DOM element. A comment containing angle brackets is displayed as text. Assigning untrusted content to innerHTML would instead ask the browser to interpret markup.

## Picture it another way

A quotation printed in a book should remain a quotation. It should not become an instruction that changes how the printing press operates.

## A common mistake

Validation that blocks one suspicious substring is not a robust replacement for context-appropriate output handling. Different output contexts have different rules.

## Try a small exercise

If a comment is meant to be plain text, is innerHTML necessary to show it?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Use safe text rendering such as textContent or normal framework interpolation. Only introduce HTML parsing when the product actually requires supported rich content and handles it safely.

cards.front: Why can cookie-based login need protection against cross-site request forgery?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

## A worked example

A settings update using ambient session cookies needs more than "a valid cookie was present." A server-verified CSRF token or another well-designed framework defense helps establish that the mutation came through the intended interaction.

## Picture it another way

A courier wearing your office badge might carry a form that someone else prepared. The badge alone does not show that you intended the instruction.

Do not assume CORS or a hidden button is a complete CSRF defense. The relevant risks depend on credential handling, request types, and server checks.

**No.** The attack relies on the browser attaching credentials to an induced request. That is why checking only for an existing signed-in session does not establish user intent.

cards.front: Why should an API not treat CORS as its authorization system?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

CORS tells a browser when a page from another origin may read a response, and preflight checks can affect certain cross-origin requests. It does not establish who a caller is or what records they may access. Non-browser clients do not use CORS as an access-control barrier.

## A worked example

An API configured to allow your frontend origin still needs session verification and record-level permissions. A script or command-line HTTP client can contact the endpoint directly, regardless of the browser origin allowlist.

## Picture it another way

A rule about which noticeboards may display a document is different from a rule about who is allowed to obtain the private document.

## A common mistake

Do not fix every CORS error by allowing every origin with credentials. Match the policy to the intended browser clients and keep server authorization independent.

## Try a small exercise

If curl can request an endpoint despite a restrictive CORS policy, does that prove CORS is broken?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** CORS is enforced by browsers for cross-origin page interactions. The server must independently enforce authentication and authorization for all clients.

cards.front: Why is a file extension insufficient to decide whether an upload is safe?

**No.** The extension is only a claim. Validate the permitted content, apply size and processing limits, and handle storage and serving according to the application's upload policy.

cards.front: Why should request logs avoid recording complete authorization headers?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Logs are copied, retained, and read by operational tools and people. Recording session tokens or secrets creates another place from which they can be stolen. Log useful event context while deliberately redacting credentials and unnecessary personal data.

## A worked example

For a failed API request, record a request ID, route, status, duration, and a safe error category. Avoid dumping the entire request body or headers when they may contain passwords, tokens, or private document text.

## Picture it another way

A repair log should note that a lock failed, not publish a copy of every customer's key.

## A common mistake

Masking secrets in the UI does not protect raw values already written to server logs. Redaction needs to happen before the sensitive data enters the logging pipeline.

## Try a small exercise

A bug report asks for full headers including a bearer token. What should a developer share instead?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Provide the relevant nonsensitive headers and diagnostic context with the token removed or redacted. A request ID can help authorized operators correlate the event without distributing a reusable credential.

cards.front: Why should a project review dependency updates and vulnerability reports regularly?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Libraries become part of the application's behavior and attack surface. Updates can fix security and correctness problems, but can also change behavior. Review relevant advisories, update deliberately, and run checks that exercise the parts your app actually uses.

## A worked example

A parser dependency publishes a security fix. Check whether the affected feature is used, update the dependency and lockfile, then verify parsing and error handling in your app. Record any unresolved constraints so the issue is not silently forgotten.

## Picture it another way

A rented tool still needs maintenance even though your team did not manufacture it. Outsourcing its construction does not remove responsibility for using it safely.

## A common mistake

A clean vulnerability scan is not proof that the entire app is secure. Scanners cover known issues and can miss configuration, authorization, and newly discovered problems.

## Try a small exercise

Why keep a lockfile when installing application dependencies?

<!-- recall:solution -->

It records the resolved dependency versions so installations can be reproduced more consistently. It supports controlled updates, but does not by itself guarantee that those versions are safe.

cards.front: Why is a focused pull request easier to review than several unrelated changes together?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A focused change gives the reviewer one concrete problem and a connected solution to assess. It is easier to understand its behavior, choose useful checks, and identify regressions. Large changes are sometimes necessary, but unrelated cleanup can obscure the part that changes user behavior.

## A worked example

A bug fix for saved filters includes the URL initialization change and a regression test. A broad restyling of every button would make that review harder without helping establish whether filters survive refresh.

## Picture it another way

Proofreading one revised paragraph is easier than finding it among pages of unrelated formatting edits. The important change should remain visible.

## A common mistake

Splitting code into tiny commits does not automatically create a coherent review. Keep pieces together when they are necessary to understand and safely apply one behavior change.

## Try a small exercise

What should the description of a filter-refresh fix tell a reviewer first?

<!-- recall:solution -->

State the failing trigger and the corrected behavior, then the relevant verification. That context lets the reviewer judge the code against a clear intended outcome.

cards.front: Why inspect the staged diff before making a Git commit?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A commit records the staged snapshot, which can differ from the rest of the working directory. Reviewing it checks the exact content being saved: intended edits, new files, accidental debug output, and files that should not be included.

## A worked example

```sh
git diff
git diff --staged
```

The first shows unstaged changes to tracked files. The second shows the proposed commit relative to the current commit. Untracked files also need attention through git status.

## Picture it another way

Checking a packed parcel before sealing it verifies what you are actually sending, not everything still lying on the desk.

## A common mistake

A change made after staging is not automatically included. Inspect status and stage the intended final version before committing.

## Try a small exercise

You stage a file, then edit one more line in it. Does the next commit automatically include that extra edit?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** The staged snapshot still contains the earlier version until you stage the new change. Review the staged diff to see exactly what the commit will contain.

cards.front: What useful confidence does continuous integration add after code is pushed?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

CI runs defined checks in an automated environment from the repository's committed contents. It can detect missing files, dependency issues, type errors, and test failures that a developer's local environment hid. Its value depends on the checks and environment actually configured.

## A worked example

A workflow checks out the commit, installs locked dependencies, runs type checking and tests, then builds the app. A locally generated file that was never committed may cause the clean CI build to fail, revealing an incomplete change.

## Picture it another way

A second kitchen follows the written recipe with the listed ingredients. If your first kitchen relied on an unlisted ingredient, the repeat exposes it.

## A common mistake

A green workflow only establishes that its checks passed. It does not prove every user path works or that a deployment has already completed.

## Try a small exercise

Why can an app build locally but fail in CI because of a missing file?

<!-- recall:solution -->

The local machine may contain an ignored or untracked file that the build relies on. CI starts from committed inputs, so the dependency must be checked in or reproducibly generated.

cards.front: Why pass an environment-specific service URL through configuration?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

The same application logic may run against different services in development, testing, and production. Configuration supplies those differences without requiring edits to the business logic. A server reads a configured database URL at startup and checks that it is present. Tests use an isolated database configuration; production uses its intended database. The code implementing a note query does not hardcode either destination.

One radio can tune to different stations. Its circuitry does not need to be rebuilt for each frequency.

Configuration can be injected at build time or runtime depending on the app. Changing a host variable after building a static frontend may not change the values already bundled into it.

<!-- recall:solution -->

Tests need isolated data and may create or remove records. Pointing them at production would mix test behavior with real user data and make results unreliable.

cards.front: In Docker, how is an image different from a running container?

Data kept only in a container's writable layer is lost when that container is removed. Use appropriate persistent storage for data that must survive replacement.

cards.front: Why can a running process still be unready to serve user requests?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

An API process starts but has not loaded required configuration. It can be alive while readiness stays false. Once essential startup work finishes, the routing system may begin sending requests according to its configured readiness policy.

## A common mistake

Restarting every instance because a shared database briefly fails can worsen an outage. Design dependency checks and thresholds with the platform's behavior in mind.

Why should a readiness response not be treated as proof that every feature works?

<!-- recall:solution -->

It verifies only its chosen conditions at that moment. Feature checks, monitoring, and user-path validation provide additional evidence beyond a single health signal.

A release introduces a new search implementation behind a flag. If error rates rise, the team can disable it while investigating. A schema change used by that feature still needs compatibility with the previous code path.

Before crossing a temporary bridge, identify the route back and whether it will remain usable. Recovery planning is part of understanding the change.

## A common mistake

Redeploying old code does not undo deleted data or external effects. Plan backups, compatible migrations, and any required forward repair for those cases.

## Try a small exercise

Why might an old application version fail after a database column was removed?

<!-- recall:solution -->

It may still read or write that column. Keep schema evolution compatible through the rollout period, and treat destructive changes as separate steps after old consumers are retired.

## Plain English

A flag lets deployed code choose whether a feature is active for a defined group or environment. It can support a limited rollout and quick disablement. Both enabled and disabled paths remain part of the system until the flag is removed.

## A worked example

Deploy a new note editor with its flag off. Enable it for a small test group, observe errors and successful saves, then expand deliberately. The previous editor remains available while the rollout is being assessed.

## Picture it another way

A new lane can be built before traffic is directed into it. Opening the gate is separate from completing the construction.

## A common mistake

A frontend flag is not an authorization boundary. Users may bypass it, and the server still needs to enforce permissions. Old flags also need cleanup to avoid growing combinations.

## Try a small exercise

Why test the flag-off path as well as the new flag-on path?

<!-- recall:solution -->

The off path may serve most users during rollout and act as the recovery option. A broken fallback removes much of the flag's practical value.

cards.front: Why test restoring a backup instead of only checking that a backup file exists?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A file can exist but be incomplete, corrupt, or unusable with the recovery procedure. A restore exercise shows whether the saved data and instructions can recreate the needed state. Perform it in an isolated environment and check representative data and relationships.

## A worked example

Export a test dataset, restore it into an empty test database, and verify record counts, linked records, and important values. Also understand how recent the backup is and how long restoration takes for your recovery requirements.

## Picture it another way

A spare key is useful only if it opens the lock. Seeing a key on the hook does not prove that it fits.

## A common mistake

Do not test a restore by overwriting the live database casually. Use an environment owned by the recovery exercise and protect the backup's sensitive contents.

## Try a small exercise

What does a successful backup job fail to establish by itself?

<!-- recall:solution -->

It does not prove that the output can be restored correctly, that it contains all required data, or that recovery finishes within the needed time. Those require a restore check.

cards.front: Why compare user-relevant outcomes before and after a performance change?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

An optimization should improve a measured problem under a representative workload. Compare the relevant outcome, such as response time or memory use, while checking correctness and other costs. A faster isolated helper may not materially improve the experience.

## A worked example

A page spends most of its time downloading a large response. Making a tiny formatting loop twice as fast may barely change load time. Measure the request size and end-to-end wait to target the actual bottleneck.

## Picture it another way

Speeding up the shortest stop on a long commute rarely transforms the whole journey. Measure where the time is spent.

## A common mistake

Averages can hide slow experiences for a minority of users. Consider distributions and representative devices, and compare under similar conditions.

## Try a small exercise

If CPU time improves but database load doubles, what should the review of the optimization include?

<!-- recall:solution -->

The tradeoff and its effect on real workload. A local speed gain may shift cost elsewhere, so judge end-to-end latency, capacity, correctness, and resource use together.

cards.front: A slow Create task request gets clicked twice and produces two tasks. How do you fix the whole flow?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Disable the submit action while that form request is pending to prevent accidental clicks. Also consider retries and other clients: for operations that must create only once per logical attempt, use a server-supported idempotency key. The server coordinates that key with the stored result so repeated attempts can return the original result.

## A worked example

The form creates one request key when a new save attempt starts and reuses it if that same attempt is retried after a timeout. A later, deliberately new task gets a new key. The server enforces uniqueness and rejects reuse with different input.

## Picture it another way

A claim ticket identifies one order. Presenting the same ticket twice should retrieve the same order, while a new order needs a new ticket.

## A common mistake

A disabled button protects only this open form. It does not protect against a retry after a lost response, another tab, or two requests arriving at the server together.

## Try a small exercise

After a timed-out create, the client generates a fresh idempotency key for the retry. What goes wrong?

<!-- recall:solution -->

The server sees a new attempt and may create another record. Reuse the same key and payload when retrying that logical operation, according to the API contract.

cards.front: Two people edit the same customer record. How can the second save avoid overwriting the first?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Include a version from the record the form loaded. The server updates only if the stored version still matches. If another save has changed it, report a conflict and let the user reload or reconcile their edits. The version check and write must be one coordinated database operation.

## A worked example

An update can use WHERE id = :id AND version = :oldVersion and set version = version + 1. If no allowed row matches, the server determines whether the record changed or no longer exists. The form keeps its draft while showing the conflict.

## Picture it another way

A checkout slip records which edition you borrowed. You cannot silently replace the current edition with handwritten changes based on an older one.

## A common mistake

Checking the version in one request and updating unconditionally afterward leaves a race between the two steps. Put the condition in the write or use your database's concurrency mechanism.

## Try a small exercise

An edit form loaded version 7, but the server now has version 8. Should it automatically overwrite version 8?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Show a conflict and help the user compare or reload. Blindly retrying the stale draft removes the protection and can discard the other person's changes.

cards.front: Two registration requests both check that an email is unused, then both insert it. What prevents duplicates?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A pre-check can improve feedback, but it cannot guarantee uniqueness while requests overlap. Define the intended uniqueness rule and enforce it with a database constraint or unique index. Catch the constraint failure and translate it into an appropriate, understandable application response.

## A worked example

If the application uses a normalized email field as its account identifier, enforce uniqueness on that stored identifier. Both requests may pass an earlier availability check, but the database admits only one conflicting value.

## Picture it another way

Two clerks can both see an empty seat on an old printout. A central reservation system must decide who actually gets the seat at the moment of booking.

## A common mistake

Be explicit about normalization and scope. Unique within one organization differs from unique across the entire application. Do not assume every email comparison rule is interchangeable.

## Try a small exercise

Can a "Check availability" endpoint replace a database uniqueness rule?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Another request can claim the value after the check. Treat the check as feedback and the database constraint as the final enforcement at write time.

cards.front: A user types "cat", then "caterer", but the screen ends up showing results for "cat". Why?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Requests can finish in a different order from the order they started. The earlier search may be slower and arrive last. Associate results with the active query or request generation and apply only the current result. Cancel obsolete requests where supported to avoid unnecessary work.

## A worked example

Request A searches cat. Request B searches caterer and finishes first. If B is the current request, ignore A when it eventually finishes. Loading and error state should also belong to the active request, so A cannot clear B's spinner or replace B's error.

## Picture it another way

You ask two assistants for different reports. The report delivered last is not necessarily the report you requested most recently.

## A common mistake

Debouncing reduces how often requests start; it does not guarantee their completion order. An old in-flight request can still finish after the latest one.

## Try a small exercise

Does waiting 300 milliseconds before issuing each search fully prevent stale results?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** It reduces request volume but does not order responses. Use cancellation and/or a current-request check before updating results, errors, and loading state.

cards.front: Why is saving every property from a profile request into the user row dangerous?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

An incoming object can contain fields that the form never offered. Build an update command from explicitly allowed fields and validate each one. Sensitive fields such as owner IDs, account roles, and approval status must come from trusted logic or separate authorized operations.

## A worked example

A profile edit accepts displayName and bio. Construct an update containing only those fields. If the body also contains isAdmin: true, that value must not become part of the database update.

## Picture it another way

A change-of-address form authorizes changing an address. Writing "make me the manager" in the margin should not grant the clerk authority to change your job title.

## A common mistake

Hiding a field in the interface is not a defense: callers can construct JSON directly. Likewise, a broad Partial<User> type is not a runtime allowlist.

## Try a small exercise

The browser sends ownerId along with a new note. Which value should determine ownership?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Derive ownership from the authenticated server context or an explicitly authorized sharing workflow. Do not let an arbitrary request body choose whose data the note belongs to.

cards.front: What must you decide before allowing deletion of a project that still has tasks?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Choose a product rule for dependent records. You might block deletion until tasks are moved, delete the tasks too, or retain an archived parent. Enforce the chosen rule with the database relationship and application behavior, and explain the effect before the user confirms.

## A worked example

If deleting a project should delete its tasks, a suitable foreign-key cascade can enforce that relationship. If tasks must survive, prevent the deletion or move them through an allowed workflow. Related changes that must succeed together belong in one transaction.

## Picture it another way

Removing a binder also affects the pages inside it. Decide whether the pages are destroyed, moved, or kept with an archived binder before taking it off the shelf.

## A common mistake

Deleting the parent in one request and children in later requests can leave a partial result. Do not add a cascade without checking which records it will remove.

## Try a small exercise

A project DELETE fails with a foreign-key violation. What should you investigate first?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Inspect which child rows reference that project and the relationship's delete rule. Then implement the intended product behavior instead of disabling the constraint to force the deletion.

cards.front: In a partial profile update, how can an omitted phone field differ from phone: null?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A partial-update contract can define omission as leaving a value unchanged and explicit null as clearing it. The server must preserve that distinction when validating and building its update. An empty string is a third input whose meaning should also be defined rather than guessed.

## A worked example

Stored phone is "555-0100". A body containing only displayName keeps that phone. A body containing phone: null clears it if the field is nullable and the API allows clearing it.

## Picture it another way

Leaving an instruction box blank can mean "do nothing to this field." Writing "erase this value" is a separate instruction with a different result.

## A common mistake

Using incoming.phone ?? existing.phone treats null like omission and prevents clearing. Conversely, filling every missing property with null can erase values the user never intended to change.

## Try a small exercise

A PATCH request changes only a biography, but the server clears the address too. What may be wrong?

<!-- recall:solution -->

The server likely converted omitted fields into empty or null values. Apply only supplied, permitted fields and handle explicit clearing according to the update contract.

cards.front: The API saved a task successfully, but the task list still shows the old title. What should you check?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

The screen may be showing a cached copy that was never updated or invalidated. Decide which views depend on the changed record. ## A worked example

A task changes from open to completed. Remove it from an open-only list or refetch that list after success. Also update its detail view and counts if they are displayed. Replacing just the title in one unrelated list is not enough.

## Picture it another way

Changing the master address book does not automatically update every printed contact sheet. Each copy needs to be replaced or refreshed.

## A common mistake

Do not indiscriminately clear all application data after every save. Target the records and queries affected by the mutation, and handle refetch failures without claiming the save failed.

## Try a small exercise

A completed task still appears under the "Open" filter after a successful save. Is changing its checkbox enough?

<!-- recall:solution -->

No. Membership in the filtered list changed too. Update the list consistently or refetch it using the active filter, and refresh any affected totals.

cards.front: What would a useful end-to-end test for editing a task verify?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Start from a known task, open its edit form, change an allowed value, and save. Verify the displayed result and reload to confirm the change was persisted. Add focused failure coverage for invalid input and access rules, rather than treating a visible success toast as proof of correctness.

## A worked example

Create a task named Draft. Edit it to Ready, wait for the save response, and reload the page. Ready should still appear on the same task ID. In a separate API test, a different user should not be able to edit that task.

## Picture it another way

Testing a light switch means checking that the lamp lights up, not just that the switch makes a clicking sound. A toast is a signal; the persisted behavior is the outcome.

## A common mistake

A test that mocks every write and checks only for "Saved" can pass while the database update is broken. Keep component tests for UI details and at least one integrated check for persistence.

## Try a small exercise

An edit test passes until it reloads the page, then the old title returns. What does that reveal?

<!-- recall:solution -->

The visible update was not successfully persisted or reloaded from the expected storage. Trace the request, response, database write, and subsequent read instead of only adjusting the toast.

Create a task named Draft. Edit it to Ready, wait for the save response, and reload the page. Ready should still appear on the same task ID. In a separate API test, a different user should not be able to edit that task.

## Picture it another way

Testing a light switch means checking that the lamp lights up, not just that the switch makes a clicking sound. A toast is a signal; the persisted behavior is the outcome.

## A common mistake

A test that mocks every write and checks only for "Saved" can pass while the database update is broken. Keep component tests for UI details and at least one integrated check for persistence.
